sidebarDescription: Follow one TimeClock outcome across repository, service, API, and UI boundaries and choose the vocabulary each caller needs.
connection: Sessions 09, 12, 17, 20, and 24 introduced Try/out, nullable lookup results, bool outcomes, and exceptions separately. This optional synthesis helps you choose among those contracts without adding outcome-design theory to Session 20.
objectives: Choose a small outcome contract based on what the caller genuinely needs.
Distinguish expected absence, ordinary rejection, structured business outcomes, and exceptional failure.
Explain why repository, service, API, and UI boundaries may translate the same event differently.
Separate temporary planning notes from permanent executable tests.

visuals.title: One event crosses several boundaries
visuals.explanation: A repository miss can become a service outcome, an HTTP response, and finally a user-facing message. Each boundary reports what its own caller needs.

visuals.title: Expected outcome or exceptional failure?
visuals.explanation: Expected absence and ordinary rejection belong in normal control flow; broken invariants and unexpected failures may justify exceptions.

visuals.title: Return the smallest useful contract
visuals.explanation: Use bool when yes or no is enough, nullable when absence is expected, and a structured result when callers need several outcome details.

visuals.title: Tests preserve settled decisions
visuals.explanation: Temporary comments help enumerate possibilities; focused tests permanently protect the outcomes the team agrees must remain true.

preQuiz.prompt: A repository lookup may normally find no open entry. Which contract communicates that expected absence directly?
preQuiz.explanation: A nullable return makes expected absence part of normal control flow.

preQuiz.prompt: Must an API expose the service's bool return value unchanged?
options: No; the API translates outcomes into its own HTTP contract
Yes; every layer must return the same type
preQuiz.explanation: Each boundary communicates with a different caller and may need a different representation.

preQuiz.prompt: When should temporary requirement comments become tests?
options: When the behavior becomes a lasting contract worth verifying
Every comment must become a test
preQuiz.explanation: Planning notes help while deciding; permanent tests preserve agreed behavior.

concept.title: Choose by semantics, not syntax preference
paragraphs: The question is not which C# feature looks most professional. Ask what happened, what the caller must know, and whether the outcome is expected during ordinary operation. Each layer reports outcomes using the vocabulary of that layer.
Guard clauses and early returns are already practiced throughout the course. They keep invalid paths short, but they do not decide which public contract a method should expose.

rows: The caller needs only accepted or rejected
Not found is expected and no explanation is required
One of several fixed named outcomes is enough
The caller needs status plus structured details
A conventional Try API must return success plus a value
An invariant is broken, input violates the contract, or an unexpected failure occurred
Attempting to complete an already completed entry
An API must report the outcome through HTTP

concept.title: Layers translate outcomes
paragraphs: Do not force one return type through every layer. A repository reports storage-shaped facts; a service reports use-case meaning; an API translates known outcomes into HTTP; a UI presents actionable language to a person.

Use one evolving TimeClock event: a duplicate clock-in. A repository may return an existing open ClockEntry, the service may return false or AlreadyClockedIn, the API may return HTTP 409 Conflict, and the UI may say You are already clocked in. None of those layers needs to leak its exact representation into the others.

rows: Entity, nullable entity, sequence, or persistence failure
Host such as App or Web
Value, bool, enum, Result object, or meaningful exception
Validation state, disabled action, or user-facing message

concept.title: Comments help plan; tests preserve contracts
paragraphs: Before implementation, a short outcome table or temporary comments can turn prose requirements into explicit cases. Remove planning comments once names, control flow, and tests communicate the decision clearly.
When an outcome must remain true, express it as a permanent test. Session 29 formalizes Arrange, Act, and Assert; this sidebar only connects that testing practice to outcome design.

concept.title: What should I actually remember?
paragraphs: Prioritize the outcome forms you will write often. Recognize specialized parameter contracts without forcing yourself to design new APIs around them from memory.

rows: bool, nullable returns, guard clauses, exceptions for clear contract violations
Enums and small Result objects for multiple business outcomes
Try/out when an existing .NET API uses it
Custom ref/in/out APIs and elaborate generic Result frameworks

lab.objective: Classify realistic TimeClock outcomes, trace one outcome across boundaries, and make one small contract improvement.
lab.startingCondition: Complete Session 24 first. This optional exercise uses notes or ScratchPad only and changes no required TimeClock production behavior.

labs.title: Choose and Translate an Outcome
labs.objective: Practice judgment rather than memorizing every possible return syntax.
labs.task: Classify several outcomes, then trace one duplicate clock-in from repository fact to service result, HTTP status, and UI message.
labs.comment: // Side Lab 24B - Choose and Translate an Outcome
instructions: Create a temporary three-column note labeled event, expected or exceptional, and caller needs.
Classify these events: no open entry found, duplicate clock-in rejected, completed entry requested twice, and database unavailable.
For each event, select the smallest suitable contract from bool, nullable return, enum, Result object, Try/out, or exception.
Choose duplicate clock-in and trace it through repository, service, API, and UI boundaries.
Write one sentence explaining why the representations do not have to be identical across those boundaries.
Sketch a small ClockInOutcome enum containing Success and AlreadyClockedIn; do not modify ClockEntryService in this optional lab.
Describe the test names you would add if the team adopted that enum permanently.
Delete or archive the temporary planning note after preserving any agreed behavior as test cases.
labs.solution: A reasonable classification is: repository cannot find an open entry — nullable ClockEntry because absence is expected; duplicate clock-in — bool when the caller needs only yes/no, or ClockInOutcome when it needs a named reason; completing an already completed entry — exception because the object invariant is violated; database unavailable — exception that the application boundary logs and translates appropriately. Across layers, AlreadyClockedIn might be an enum value in the service, an HTTP 409 response in the API, and a clear user-facing message in the UI. Suggested permanent tests: TryClockIn_WhenEntryIsAlreadyOpen_ReturnsAlreadyClockedIn and TryClockIn_WhenNoEntryIsOpen_ReturnsSuccess.

lab.expectedBehavior: You can justify a contract from semantics and explain how later boundaries translate the same outcome for different callers.
lab.validation: No build is required; this optional sidebar changes no production files.

commit: Not applicable — optional judgment exercise with no required source changes.
review: Ordinary absence is not modeled as an exception without a specific reason.
A bool is used only when the caller genuinely needs no explanation.
Try/out is recognized as a common .NET pattern rather than the default for new application APIs.
Repository details do not leak directly into API or UI contracts.
Temporary planning notes are not mistaken for permanent documentation or tests.

postQuiz.prompt: When is a Result object more useful than bool?
options: When callers need structured status or details beyond yes/no
postQuiz.explanation: Do not add a Result object unless its additional information serves callers.

postQuiz.prompt: Should a missing database connection become a normal nullable entity result?
options: No; infrastructure failure is different from an expected not-found result
Yes; null means every kind of failure
postQuiz.explanation: Conflating failure with absence hides an operational problem.

postQuiz.prompt: Why might a service enum become an HTTP 409 at the API boundary?
options: The API translates business meaning into its caller's protocol
postQuiz.explanation: HTTP is the API caller's contract, not necessarily the service's internal representation.

reflections: Which current TimeClock bool would become clearer if callers needed to distinguish two rejection reasons?
Where would returning null accidentally hide a real system failure?
Which outcome decisions deserve permanent tests rather than explanatory comments?
whatBreaks: Skipping this sidebar does not break Session 25. You would lose only the practical synthesis for choosing and translating method outcomes across application boundaries.
summary: Choose outcomes by semantics and caller needs: bool for simple yes/no, nullable for expected absence, enums or Result objects for named or structured business outcomes, Try/out mainly for established Try patterns, and exceptions for violated contracts or unexpected failures. Translate outcomes at repository, service, API, and UI boundaries instead of leaking one representation everywhere.
